You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

– the failing test (signature + snippet),

Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: 
- What the failing test does
  - It defines a strictly increasing, convex function f(x) = exp(x) − π^3 whose root is at x* = ln(π^3) ≈ 3.4341896575482003.
  - It constructs a RegulaFalsiSolver and calls solve with the bracketing interval [1, 10] and a high evaluation cap (3624).
  - The test is annotated with @Test(expected=TooManyEvaluationsException.class), i.e. it expects the solver to fail to converge and throw, which is the behavior historically associated with the classic “false position” method on such convex functions (Commons Math issue MATH-631).

- Relevant code wiring
  - RegulaFalsiSolver() simply selects the REGULA_FALSI variant in the base implementation:
    - RegulaFalsiSolver(): calls super(DEFAULT_ABSOLUTE_ACCURACY, Method.REGULA_FALSI).
  - BaseSecantSolver stores that “method” choice and its solve overloads delegate to a common core with a default start value (the midpoint) and AllowedSolution.ANY_SIDE:
    - solve(maxEval, f, min, max): returns solve(maxEval, f, min, max, min + 0.5*(max-min), AllowedSolution.ANY_SIDE).

- Why the failure occurs
  - The “classic” Regula Falsi (false position) update uses the secant formula to compute the next x between the bracket endpoints, then replaces the endpoint having the same sign as f(x). On strictly convex/concave monotonic functions, one endpoint can remain almost fixed while only the other moves; progress in shrinking the bracket length can become extremely slow (the “sticky endpoint” problem).
  - For f(x) = exp(x) − π^3 on [1, 10], the method keeps replacing the lower bound repeatedly while the upper bound stays effectively unchanged for a long time due to convexity. The function value at the moving endpoint decreases only geometrically and may not reach the functionValueAccuracy threshold within the allowed number of evaluations.
  - Because RegulaFalsiSolver selects Method.REGULA_FALSI (as shown above) and, in that mode, the core loop does not apply any of the convergence-accelerating tweaks (e.g., Illinois or Pegasus rescaling of the “stuck” endpoint’s function value), the algorithm stalls and eventually exhausts the evaluation budget, throwing TooManyEvaluationsException. This is exactly the scenario described in the current bug report and historically tracked as MATH-631.

- How this maps to the observed test and report
  - The bug report snippet (solve(100, f, 1, 10)) “fails with …” (the truncated text is consistent with TooManyEvaluationsException) because 100 evaluations are not enough for the unmodified Regula Falsi to reach its tight stopping criteria on this function/interval.
  - The failing test in question explicitly expects TooManyEvaluationsException for essentially the same setup, which is consistent with the above analysis of the algorithm’s behavior. The inclusion of an equality assertion after the solve call is dead code under the expected-exception annotation; the test is demonstrating the known failure mode rather than verifying a successful solve.

In short: The RegulaFalsiSolver delegates to a base implementation configured to use the classic “false position” algorithm. On the convex function exp(x) − π^3 over [1, 10], that algorithm suffers from the “stuck endpoint” pathology, fails to sufficiently reduce either the bracket or the function value within the evaluation limit, and throws TooManyEvaluationsException. This is the cause of the failure reported and of the behavior exercised by the test.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
